chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who said: He wrote to me on a piece of paper:

O Allah! Return to all of Your creatures their grievances that are due from me, their small ones and their big ones, with ease from You and well-being. And what my strength cannot reach, and what the extent of my hand cannot encompass, and what my body and conviction and self are not strong enough to bear, therefore settle it for me from the abundance of what is with You from Your Grace. Then do not leave behind upon me anything from it; settle it from my good deeds, O Most Merciful of the merciful ones.

I testify that there is no god except Allah, Alone, with no partner for Him. And I testify that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger. And that the Religion is as it was legislated, and that Islam is as it was described, and that the Book is as it was revealed, and that the Words are as they were narrated, and that Allah is the Clear Truth.
May Allah mention Muhammad and his Household with goodness, and greet Muhammad and his Household with peace.

key_terms.أَرْحَمَ الرَّاحِمِينَ: The Most Merciful of the merciful ones
key_terms.مَظَالِمُ: Grievances or rights owed to others, particularly financial or personal dues

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia supplication for settling debts and grievances owed to others?
ai.summary: Recorded in Al-Kafi, this supplication from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) addresses the spiritual burden of 'mazalim' (rights of people), emphasizing that settling these debts is crucial for divine acceptance. It uniquely proposes a mechanism where Allah compensates for the supplicant's inability to repay through His abundant grace, while any shortfall is deducted from the believer's accumulated good deeds. This reflects the Shia emphasis on interpersonal rights as a prerequisite for spiritual purity and final judgment.
